name: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
title: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
answer: Timekeeping and billing narratives covers the systems and practices that turn recorded work into the descriptions clients pay for, from the timer a lawyer starts before a call to the invoice line that reaches the client. It sits inside legal operations because the output feeds billing, budgeting and matter review, and it touches security because the underlying records are privileged and confidential. The topic spans the capture of time, the drafting of narrative text, the review of entries before they are sent, and the reconciliation of billed hours against budgets and estimates.

sections.body: Timekeeping and billing narratives covers the systems and practices that turn recorded work into the descriptions clients pay for, from the timer a lawyer starts before a call to the invoice line that reaches the client. It sits inside legal operations because the output feeds billing, budgeting and matter review, and it touches security because the underlying records are privileged and confidential. The topic spans the capture of time, the drafting of narrative text, the review of entries before they are sent, and the reconciliation of billed hours against budgets and estimates.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on time capture tools such as timers embedded in practice management and e-billing platforms, on document and email systems that supply context for an entry, and increasingly on language models that draft or tidy narrative text. Firms with mature operations keep a single source of truth for time records, usually the practice management system, and push approved entries into e-billing platforms that clients and outside counsel guidelines require. Access controls, audit logs and retention rules matter here because a time entry can reveal client identity, matter strategy and fee exposure.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners capture time close to the event, then convert raw notes into short narratives that state the task, the person who did it and why it mattered to the matter. Reviewers check entries against outside counsel guidelines, block billing rules and task codes before submission, and billing staff reconcile the result with budgets and prior estimates. Language models are used to expand terse notes into readable descriptions, to standardise phrasing across a team and to flag entries that look vague, duplicated or inconsistent with the matter phase, with a human approving anything that reaches a client.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on accuracy, privilege and client trust: a narrative that overstates work or hides who performed it creates fee disputes and, in serious cases, regulatory exposure. Firms set rules for who may edit an entry, how AI-assisted drafts are labelled internally, and how long raw time records are kept, and they align those rules with outside counsel guidelines and e-billing requirements. Provenance matters because a client may ask how a figure was reached, so the link between the original note, the edit history and the final invoice line should be reconstructable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter coupling between time capture and matter budgeting, with entries checked against estimates as they are written rather than after the invoice is issued. AI drafting of narratives will become routine, which shifts the reviewer's job toward sampling, exception handling and guideline enforcement rather than line-by-line rewriting. The open questions are how much of the drafting record clients should see, how firms evidence that a narrative is accurate, and whether alternative fee arrangements reduce the volume of narrative text that has to be produced at all.
